questions.stem: Which of the following is quantitative data?
options: The employee ID assigned to each staff member
The postcode recorded against each delivery address
The number of units sold per store per week
The written text of a customer's product review
questions.explanation: Quantitative data is numerical, measurable and countable, and answers how many / how much / how often. (A) and (B) are the traps — both are written in digits, but neither supports meaningful arithmetic, so both are qualitative (nominal) data.

questions.stem: A dataset records each store's postcode as a four-digit number. What level of measurement is postcode?
options: Interval
Ordinal
Nominal
Ratio
questions.explanation: Nominal — A postcode is a label, not a quantity — averaging postcodes produces a meaningless number. The exam trap is assuming digits imply quantitative data. Test: does arithmetic on it mean anything?

questions.stem: Temperature in degrees Celsius is an example of which level of measurement?
options: Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio
questions.explanation: Interval — It has order and equal intervals, but zero is arbitrary (0 °C does not mean "no temperature"). This is why 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C — ratios are invalid. Kelvin, by contrast, is ratio, because 0 K is a true zero.

questions.stem: Which statistic is the most appropriate measure of centre for Likert-scale responses?
options: The median, since the data is ordinal
The mean, since the responses are recorded as numbers 1–5
The mode, since only the most frequently chosen response is meaningful
The mean of the middle three response levels, excluding the extremes
questions.explanation: Median — Likert data is ordinal — ordered, but with intervals that are not known to be equal — so the mean assumes a precision the data does not have. The mode is also valid, which is why (C) is tempting; it is rejected because it overstates the case, not because the mode is wrong.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to know why checkout abandonment rose. Which approach is best?
options: Segment the existing transaction data by device, time of day and basket value
Increase the sample size of the existing transaction dataset
Collect qualitative data through exit surveys and user interviews
Convert the existing categorical fields to a ratio level of measurement
questions.explanation: (A) is the strongest distractor — segmentation is real, useful analysis, and it will tell you which customers abandon and when. It still cannot tell you why. Quantitative data gives the what (abandonment is 42%); qualitative gives the why (shipping cost appears too late). A mixed-methods answer is the strongest exam response.

questions.stem: In the DIKW model, what distinguishes information from data?
options: Information is numerical, whereas data may be text, image or audio
Information has been processed, organised and placed in context
Information has been stored in a structured database rather than a flat file
Information has been verified as accurate, whereas data has not
questions.explanation: Data is raw, unprocessed facts with no context. (D) is the subtle one: accuracy is a quality attribute that applies at every level of DIKW — inaccurate information is still information. Knowledge then applies information to make decisions; wisdom applies judgement.

questions.stem: Informatics is best defined as:
options: The statistical techniques used to summarise and describe the contents of a dataset
The transformation of data into information and knowledge to support decision-making, including the people, processes and technology involved
The design of the hardware and network infrastructure on which enterprise data is stored
The visual presentation of statistical results so that decision-makers can interpret them
questions.explanation: The people and processes clause is what separates informatics from the purely technical options. (A) is statistics and (D) is data visualisation — both are components of informatics rather than definitions of it.

questions.stem: Which is an example of semi-structured data?
options: A JSON file returned by a weather API
A relational database table of sales records
A CSV export of that same sales table
A recorded customer phone call
questions.explanation: JSON has tags and markers giving it some organisation, but no rigid predefined schema, and records may carry different fields. (C) is the near-miss — a CSV has fixed columns for every row, which makes it structured despite being a plain text file. (D) is unstructured.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of enterprise data is typically unstructured, and why does this matter?
options: About half — with the remainder being semi-structured rather than structured
The large majority — but it can be queried with conventional SQL once it has been indexed
A small minority — the bulk of enterprise data sits in relational systems
The large majority — it requires ML, NLP or computer vision rather than SQL to analyse
questions.explanation: (B) shares the correct first half and fails on the second, which is where the reasoning mark sits. Email, documents, images, video, audio and social posts cannot be queried conventionally, which is a major driver of data-lake architectures and AI adoption.

questions.stem: A number identifying a player's jersey is best classified as:
options: Nominal, because it functions purely as a label
Ordinal, because squad numbers are allocated in order of seniority
Interval, because the gap between consecutive numbers is equal
Ratio, because it is numeric and has a meaningful zero
questions.explanation: Nominal — Each distractor states the genuine defining property of its own level — which is what makes them plausible. The digit here is an identifier only: jersey 10 plus jersey 4 is not jersey 14, and jersey 20 is not "twice" jersey 10.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly describes CCTV footage captured automatically for security?
options: Manual and passive
Computerised and active
Computerised and passive
Manual and active
questions.explanation: Computerised because a system captures it without an operator; passive because the subject does not knowingly engage in the collection. The two axes are independent — check each separately rather than treating "automatic" as settling both.

questions.stem: The main advantage of active data collection over passive collection is:
options: Participants consent and can explain their reasoning, giving context to the response
It captures behaviour as it actually happens, without relying on the participant's recall
It produces far larger volumes of data at a lower cost per record
It removes the risk of response bias, because answers are supplied directly by the subject
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are passive collection's advantages, and (D) is backwards — response bias is a risk created by asking people questions. Active collection can capture why; its costs are that it is slow, expensive and produces small samples.

questions.stem: A researcher splits a population into age brackets and samples proportionally from each. This is:
options: Cluster sampling
Stratified sampling
Systematic sampling
Quota sampling
questions.explanation: Stratified — The population is divided into strata and sampled in proportion, guaranteeing each subgroup is represented. (D) is the fine distinction: quota sampling also fills subgroup targets, but selects non-randomly within each one, so it does not support statistical inference.

questions.stem: A quality-control officer tests every 50th item off the production line. This is:
options: Systematic
Simple random
Stratified
Cluster
questions.explanation: Systematic — Every nth record is selected from an ordered list. It is simple and cheap, but risks periodic bias if the production cycle happens to align with the sampling interval — for example if every 50th item comes off the same machine head.

questions.stem: The greatest weakness of convenience sampling is:
options: The resulting sample is too small to support statistical inference
It requires a complete sampling frame, which is rarely available in practice
The sample is unlikely to represent the population, producing selection bias
It cannot be used to collect quantitative data
questions.explanation: (B) is the requirement of random sampling — convenience sampling needs no frame at all, which is precisely why it gets used. Sampling whoever is easiest to reach systematically excludes those who are harder to reach.

questions.stem: In RAVR, validity asks:
options: Is the data close to the true value?
Is the data measuring what it claims to measure?
Would repeating the method give consistent results?
Is the data related to the question being asked?
questions.explanation: Validity = measuring the right construct. (A) is accuracy, (C) is reliability, (D) is relevance — all four RAVR terms appear as options, so this must be answered on the definition. A bathroom scale reading 2 kg heavy every time is reliable but not accurate.

questions.stem: A set of scales consistently reads 3 kg too high. The data is:
options: Reliable but not accurate
Accurate but not reliable
Both accurate and reliable
Neither accurate nor reliable
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency of the method; accuracy is closeness to the true value. A systematic offset is perfectly repeatable and perfectly wrong — which is why reliability alone is never evidence of quality.

questions.stem: An operator types 1243 instead of 1234. This is a:
options: Transcription error
Transposition error
Truncation error
Rounding error
questions.explanation: Transposition — Two adjacent characters have been swapped. (A) is the broader category of general mistyping, so it is not wrong so much as insufficiently specific — and check digits are designed specifically to catch transpositions.

questions.stem: Which validation check would prevent a date of birth of 2099-01-01 from being accepted?
options: Check digit
Format check
Type check
Range check
questions.explanation: Range check — It confirms the value falls within acceptable limits — here, that the date is not in the future. The value passes a type check (it is a valid date) and a format check (it matches YYYY-MM-DD), which is exactly why those two are insufficient.

questions.stem: The distinction between validation and verification of data entry is:
options: Validation checks that data matches the source; verification checks it is reasonable and correctly formed
Validation checks whether data is reasonable and correctly formed at entry; verification checks it matches the source
Validation is performed automatically by the system; verification is always performed manually
Validation is applied before storage; verification is applied after retrieval
questions.explanation: Validation = "is this sensible and correctly formed?" (range, type, presence, format, check digit). Verification = "is this what was on the source?" (double entry, proofreading). (C) describes a common tendency, not the definition — and validated data can still be completely wrong.

questions.stem: An outlier in a dataset should first be:
options: Replaced with the median, which is far less sensitive to extreme values
Removed, since a single extreme value distorts both the mean and the standard deviation
Investigated to determine whether it is an error or a genuine extreme value
Retained, but excluded from any summary statistic that assumes a normal distribution
questions.explanation: (D) is the sophisticated trap — it is a defensible treatment, but it still skips the investigation, and the word in the stem is first. Deleting outliers without investigating destroys real signal: fraud, equipment failure and your best customer all look like outliers. Any treatment applied must be documented and justified.

questions.stem: Which is an example of response bias?
options: Survey respondents overstating how often they exercise
A survey distributed only to customers who already visit the website
A sensor that has gradually drifted out of calibration
A model trained on data that under-represents one group of customers
questions.explanation: Response bias is participants answering what looks good rather than what is true — also called social-desirability bias. (B) is selection bias, (C) measurement bias and (D) algorithmic bias; all four are named bias types, so the categories must be distinguished rather than eliminated.

questions.stem: An enterprise trains a recruitment model on ten years of its own hiring decisions, which favoured one demographic. The model reproduces that pattern. This is:
options: Measurement bias, since the historical records were captured inconsistently over the decade
Algorithmic bias arising from biased training data
Selection bias, since only successful applicants appear in the training dataset
Confirmation bias, since the enterprise chose a model that confirmed its existing practice
questions.explanation: (C) is the sharpest near-miss — it describes a real structural problem with hiring datasets, but the stem says the model reproduces a demographic pattern present in past decisions, which is bias inherited through the data. The model now automates historical discrimination at scale with a veneer of objectivity. Mitigations: representative data, bias auditing, fairness metrics, diverse teams, ongoing monitoring.

questions.stem: Which is metadata rather than data?
options: The name of the product being reviewed
The star rating the customer selected
The text the customer wrote in the review
The date and time at which the review was submitted
questions.explanation: Metadata is data about data — author, timestamp, file size, geotag, schema, device. Note that metadata alone is often sufficient to identify and profile a person, which is why it is privacy-relevant even when the content is not disclosed.

questions.stem: A dataset contains the same customer twice under slightly different spellings of their name. The most appropriate treatment is:
options: Retain both records, since deleting either risks losing genuine transactions
Deduplicate using fuzzy matching during the data cleaning stage
Retain the more recent record and delete the older one
Standardise the name formats, after which the duplicates will merge automatically
questions.explanation: (D) is the trap for anyone who has done a little cleaning: standardising case and punctuation will not reconcile "Smith" with "Smyth", and nothing merges automatically. (C) silently discards the older record's transaction history. Duplicates inflate counts, distort averages and break customer-level analysis.

questions.stem: Secondary data's most significant limitation is that:
options: It costs more to obtain than primary data of comparable scale
It is always less current than data the enterprise collects for itself
The collection methodology was chosen by someone else and often cannot be verified
It is usually unstructured, so it requires far more cleaning before use
questions.explanation: You inherit someone else's sample, definitions and instrument — and it may be perfectly good data for a different question. Its advantages are speed, cost and scale, which rules out (A) directly.

questions.stem: Sampling is used instead of a census primarily because:
options: A census is often too costly, slow or impractical to conduct
A well-drawn sample is more accurate than a census of the same population
Sampling removes the bias that arises when an entire population is surveyed
Samples fall outside the ethics approval requirements that apply to a census
questions.explanation: A well-designed sample trades a known, quantifiable margin of error for enormous savings in time and cost. It does not eliminate bias — poor sampling creates it, which disposes of (C).

questions.stem: Which sampling method carries the highest sampling error for a given sample size?
options: Simple random
Cluster
Stratified
Systematic
questions.explanation: Cluster — Because whole naturally occurring groups are sampled, members within a cluster tend to resemble one another, so each additional observation adds less new information. It is chosen for cost and logistics, not for precision — stratified sampling sits at the opposite end.

questions.stem: A survey is distributed only through the enterprise's mobile app. The resulting dataset most likely suffers from:
options: Confirmation bias
Response bias
Measurement bias
Coverage/selection bias
questions.explanation: App-only distribution systematically excludes non-users — often older, lower-income or less digitally connected customers — so the sample cannot represent the whole customer base. The fault is in who was asked, not in how they answered, which is what separates it from (B).

questions.stem: "Garbage in, garbage out" in a data science context means:
options: Analysis and models can be no better than the quality of the data fed into them
Poor-quality data increases storage costs and degrades query performance
Data that has not been cleaned cannot be loaded into a data warehouse
Unstructured data cannot be analysed until it has been converted to a structured form
questions.explanation: No amount of sophisticated modelling repairs biased, inaccurate or unrepresentative input — and a sophisticated model on bad data is more dangerous, because it looks authoritative. This is why cleaning and RAVR assessment precede analysis rather than follow it.

questions.stem: What makes a blockchain tamper-evident?
options: Only nodes holding a valid certificate are permitted to append a block
Each block is encrypted with the writing participant's private key
Each block is timestamped by a trusted authority before it is appended
Each block stores the hash of the previous block
questions.explanation: Altering a block changes its hash, so the next block's stored "previous hash" no longer matches — and the break cascades forward through every subsequent block. (A) and (C) are real integrity controls, but both reintroduce a central authority, which is precisely what blockchain is designed to avoid.

questions.stem: A hash is best described as:
options: A fixed-length, one-way fingerprint of the input data
A fixed-length encryption of the input data, reversible with the correct key
A variable-length checksum whose length reflects the size of the input
A unique identifier assigned to each node on the network
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) each break exactly one defining property — a hash is one-way (you cannot recover the input) and fixed-length regardless of input size. Any change to the input, however small, produces a completely different hash.

questions.stem: A smart contract is:
options: A digital certificate binding a participant's identity to their public key
A legally binding agreement whose signed copy is stored immutably on a blockchain
The rule set determining which nodes are permitted to validate a new block
Self-executing code stored on a blockchain that runs when specified conditions are met
questions.explanation: (B) is the trap the name invites — a smart contract is code that acts, not a document that is stored. Because it executes automatically and is recorded immutably it removes the need for an intermediary, but a bug in the contract is also immutable, which is a genuine enterprise risk.

questions.stem: In a blockchain, a node is:
options: A single transaction recorded within a block
A participant computer holding a copy of the ledger
A block that has been validated but not yet appended to the chain
The cryptographic link joining one block to the next
questions.explanation: Distribution across many nodes is what makes the ledger decentralised — there is no single point of failure and no single party who can quietly rewrite it.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants tamper-evident, auditable provenance records for its coffee supply chain. Blockchain is appropriate mainly because:
options: It removes the need for participants to enter provenance data manually at each stage
It stores provenance records more cheaply than a conventional database would
It writes and retrieves transactions faster than a centralised database
It provides a shared, immutable record that no single participant can retrospectively alter
questions.explanation: The value case is trust between parties who do not fully trust each other. (B) and (C) are both false — blockchain is slower and more expensive per record. (A) is the "garbage in" caveat worth naming: blockchain guarantees the record has not been altered, not that it was true when written.

questions.stem: A consensus mechanism exists to:
options: Determine which node is permitted to hold the master copy of the ledger
Encrypt the contents of each block so that only participants can read them
Allow nodes to agree that a block is valid before it is added to the chain
Compress older blocks so the chain consumes less storage over time
questions.explanation: Examples include proof of work and proof of stake. (A) is self-contradictory in a way that is easy to miss under pressure — there is no master copy, which is the entire point. Proof of work is also what makes blockchain energy-intensive.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine limitation of blockchain for enterprise use?
options: Data cannot be shared between separate organisations without a trusted intermediary
Records cannot be independently audited, since no single party holds the complete ledger
High energy use, low transaction throughput, and the difficulty of correcting an erroneous entry
Entries cannot be timestamped, so transaction order has to be inferred from context
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are the opposite of blockchain's properties stated as though they were faults. Immutability cuts both ways: a wrong entry can only be superseded, never erased — which collides directly with the right to erasure in GDPR-style privacy law.

questions.stem: The "three Vs" of big data are:
options: Volume, Variety, Velocity
Volume, Variety, Veracity
Volume, Validity, Velocity
Value, Variety, Velocity
questions.explanation: Each distractor substitutes exactly one term, and in (B) and (D) that term is a genuine additional V. Veracity (trustworthiness) and Value (usefulness) are commonly added as a fourth and fifth, but the classic three are volume, variety and velocity.

questions.stem: A retailer must process transactions as they arrive, in real time, rather than in an overnight batch. This is a challenge of:
options: Variety
Volume
Velocity
Veracity
questions.explanation: Velocity — the speed of generation and the speed at which processing must keep up. The infrastructure implication is stream processing rather than batch, which is what enables in-the-moment decisions such as blocking a fraudulent transaction mid-authorisation.

questions.stem: A data warehouse differs from an operational database because it is:
options: Integrated, cleaned, historical and structured for analysis
Highly normalised and optimised for large numbers of small, fast writes
A raw store that retains data in its original format until a use is found for it
Restricted to a single department's subject area and reporting requirements
questions.explanation: The warehouse is the analysis layer: subject-oriented, integrated from many sources, time-variant and non-volatile. (B) describes the operational database (OLTP) it is being contrasted with, (C) a data lake, and (D) a data mart — all four storage concepts appear as options.

questions.stem: In ETL, the Transform step involves:
options: Writing the prepared data into the warehouse
Reading the required data out of the source systems
Cleaning, standardising, deduplicating and aggregating the data
Converting the stored data into charts and dashboards for decision-makers
questions.explanation: (B) is Extract and (A) is Load. Transform is where "NSW", "N.S.W." and "New South Wales" become one value, units are reconciled and business rules are applied — and where invisible editorial decisions get baked in permanently.

questions.stem: A data lake without governance becomes a:
options: Data mart
Data swamp
Data warehouse
Data cube
questions.explanation: Data swamp — raw data accumulated without catalogue, metadata, quality standards or ownership, so nobody can find anything in it or trust what they do find. Governance is what separates a lake from a swamp; the storage technology is identical.

questions.stem: A data mart is best described as:
options: A pre-aggregated multidimensional structure supporting fast slice-and-dice queries
A raw store holding data in its original format until a use is found for it
A commercial marketplace through which enterprises buy and sell datasets
A subject-specific subset of a data warehouse serving one department
questions.explanation: For example a marketing data mart drawn from the enterprise warehouse. (A) is a data cube, which is the sharpest distractor because marts are frequently implemented as cubes. Benefits: faster queries, simpler models, departmental control. Risk: marts drifting into conflicting definitions of the same measure.

questions.stem: A supermarket discovers that customers who buy nappies frequently also buy a particular snack. This is:
options: Association / market basket analysis
Clustering
Classification
Anomaly detection
questions.explanation: Association rules find items that co-occur; clustering would group the customers rather than the products. It informs product placement, bundling and recommendations — but co-occurrence is not causation, and low-support rules are usually noise.

questions.stem: Segmenting customers into previously unknown groups based on behaviour, with no predefined labels, is:
options: Classification
Clustering
Association
Regression
questions.explanation: Clustering — an unsupervised technique. (A) is the named adjacent-term trap: classification assigns records to known, predefined categories using labelled training data. The phrase "previously unknown groups" is the tell.

questions.stem: A bank flags a transaction that deviates sharply from a customer's established pattern. The data mining technique is:
options: Clustering
Classification
Anomaly detection
Association
questions.explanation: Anomaly detection — Its enterprise trade-off is the false positive: freezing a legitimate customer's card is a real cost with a real customer-service consequence, so the detection threshold is a business decision, not merely a technical one.

questions.stem: Predicting a numeric value such as next quarter's revenue from historical variables uses:
options: Anomaly detection
Classification
Clustering
Regression
questions.explanation: Regression — modelling a numeric relationship in order to predict a continuous value. Classification would instead predict a category, such as churn / no churn. The output type is what decides it.

questions.stem: Data mining is best defined as:
options: Discovering previously unknown patterns and relationships within large datasets
Extracting data from source systems and loading it into a central warehouse
Running reports and queries against a warehouse to answer questions already defined
Building predictive models from labelled historical training data
questions.explanation: The emphasis is on previously unknown — (C) is the distinction that matters most in practice: running a report you already designed is querying, not mining. (D) is supervised machine learning, one technique within mining rather than a definition of it.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest ethical objection to data mining of customer purchase histories?
options: It requires personal data to be retained for far longer than the transaction itself requires
It can infer sensitive attributes — pregnancy, illness, financial stress — that the customer never disclosed
It produces conclusions that customers cannot see, access or challenge
It analyses data collected before the enterprise's current privacy policy was in force
questions.explanation: All four are genuine concerns, but inference is the one that sidesteps consent entirely — the customer agreed to have purchases recorded, not to have a health condition deduced from them. This is the core of the "secondary use" problem in privacy law.

questions.stem: An enterprise keeps raw sensor data for 7 days and hourly aggregates for 5 years. This is an example of:
options: Tiered retention
De-identification
Data minimisation
Normalisation
questions.explanation: Tiered retention — (C) is the close relative: minimisation limits what you collect, whereas tiering governs how long each form of what you collected is kept. It balances analytical value against storage cost and supports the principle of not retaining personal data longer than necessary.

questions.stem: A foreign key is:
options: Two or more fields combined to form a single unique identifier
A field that uniquely identifies each record within its own table
A field that references the primary key of another table
A field that has been indexed in order to speed up joins between tables
questions.explanation: The foreign key is what physically creates the relationship between two tables. (B) describes a primary key, (A) a composite key and (D) an index — four different concepts that all attach to fields.

questions.stem: A student can enrol in many subjects and each subject has many students. To implement this in a relational database you need:
options: A repeating group of subject codes stored within each STUDENT record
A foreign key in STUDENT referencing SUBJECT
A foreign key in SUBJECT referencing STUDENT
A junction table with a composite primary key
questions.explanation: A relational database cannot store M:N directly, which is why (B) and (C) both fail — either one would cap the relationship at 1:M in one direction. The junction table (ENROLMENT) resolves it into two 1:M relationships and gives attributes of the relationship itself — Grade, DateEnrolled — somewhere to live.

questions.stem: Referential integrity requires that:
options: Every table in the database has a declared primary key
Every foreign key value matches an existing primary key value
No field in any table is permitted to contain a null value
Every value entered is checked against its declared data type
questions.explanation: It prevents "orphan" records — an order pointing at a customer who does not exist. Enforced by the DBMS through cascade or restrict rules on delete and update. (A) is a precondition for it rather than the rule itself.

questions.stem: Normalisation primarily aims to:
options: Speed up every query by reducing the volume of data that must be scanned
Reduce redundancy, and with it the update anomalies that redundancy causes
Reduce the physical size of the database file stored on disk
Ensure that every foreign key points at a record that actually exists
questions.explanation: (A) is the seductive one and is close to backwards: the trade-off is that heavily normalised schemas require more joins, which is exactly why analytical warehouses are deliberately denormalised into star schemas for query speed. (D) is referential integrity.

questions.stem: Which SQL clause filters rows before aggregation?
options: WHERE
HAVING
GROUP BY
ORDER BY
questions.explanation: WHERE — HAVING filters after GROUP BY has aggregated. The classic exam distinction: WHERE amount > 100 filters individual rows; HAVING SUM(amount) > 100 filters whole groups — and the two produce very different results on the same data.

questions.stem: SELECT Suburb, COUNT() FROM Customer GROUP BY Suburb ORDER BY COUNT() DESC; returns:
options: A single row containing the total number of customers
The number of customers in each suburb, in alphabetical order of suburb
Every customer's record, sorted by suburb
The number of customers in each suburb, most populous suburb first
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses the rows into one per suburb, COUNT() counts the members of each group, and ORDER BY COUNT() DESC sorts by that count, largest first. (B) is what you would get with ORDER BY Suburb; (A) is what you would get with no GROUP BY at all.

questions.stem: Which SQL operation combines rows from two tables based on a matching key?
options: JOIN
UNION
MERGE
INTERSECT
questions.explanation: JOIN — UNION stacks two result sets vertically and requires matching columns; INTERSECT returns rows common to both; MERGE inserts or updates based on a match rather than returning a combined result. Only JOIN widens rows horizontally by matching a key.

questions.stem: In crow's foot notation, the "crow's foot" symbol at one end of a relationship line indicates:
options: Optional, or zero
One
Many
Mandatory, or at least one
questions.explanation: Many — Every option names a real element of the notation: a single perpendicular bar means one, a circle means optional (zero), and a bar nearest the entity means mandatory. Combinations read as "one and only one", "zero or many", and so on — read both symbols at each end.

questions.stem: A flat file system's core weakness compared with a relational database is:
options: Data redundancy, leading to inconsistency and update anomalies
Records cannot be sorted or indexed for retrieval
It cannot represent more than one entity type within a single file
It cannot be backed up without taking the system offline
questions.explanation: The same customer's address repeated across a thousand rows means one address change requires a thousand correct edits — and any row missed makes the file internally contradictory. This is exactly the problem normalisation exists to solve.

questions.stem: A DBMS provides all of the following except:
options: Enforcement of the integrity rules declared in the schema
Controlled, role-based access to the stored data
A guarantee that the data users enter is accurate
Concurrent multi-user access managed through record locking
questions.explanation: A DBMS enforces structural correctness — type, range, referential integrity — but cannot know that a correctly formatted address is the wrong address. Validation is not truth, which is the same distinction as validation versus verification.

questions.stem: In a spreadsheet, =VLOOKUP(A2, Products!A:C, 3, FALSE) returns:
options: The value in the third column of the Products range, for an exact match on A2
The value in the third column of the Products range, for the nearest match to A2
The value in the first column of the Products range, for an exact match on A2
An error, because the lookup range must be a single column
questions.explanation: The final FALSE forces an exact match, which is almost always what you want. (B) is what TRUE would give — and on unsorted data it silently returns wrong values rather than an error, which makes it one of the most common quiet spreadsheet faults.

questions.stem: A pivot table is most useful for:
options: Highlighting cells automatically when their values meet a defined condition
Applying one formula down a whole column without rewriting it per row
Rapidly summarising and cross-tabulating a large dataset by category
Restricting the values a user is permitted to type into a cell
questions.explanation: It aggregates (sum, count, average) across chosen row and column dimensions and lets you re-orient the summary instantly — essentially OLAP-style analysis inside a spreadsheet. (A) is conditional formatting and (D) is data validation.

questions.stem: Which spreadsheet feature works backwards from a single desired result to find the one input value required to produce it?
options: Scenario Manager
Goal Seek
Solver
Data Table
questions.explanation: Goal Seek — "What unit price gives me $200,000 profit?" (C) is the near-miss: Solver also works backwards, but it optimises multiple variables subject to constraints. Scenario Manager and Data Tables extend Goal Seek into multi-variable what-if analysis.

questions.stem: A composite key is used when:
options: The table has been deliberately denormalised for query performance
The table contains one or more foreign keys
The primary key value must be generated automatically by the DBMS
No single field uniquely identifies a record
questions.explanation: In an ENROLMENT table neither StudentID nor SubjectID alone is unique, but the combination is. (B) is the tempting one — a junction table's composite key is usually made of foreign keys, but the presence of foreign keys is not itself the reason.

questions.stem: In a data dictionary, which of the following would you expect to find?
options: The queries and reports that draw on each table
The entities, their relationships, and the cardinality between them
Field name, data type, size, format, validation rule and description
The users permitted to read or modify each field
questions.explanation: (B) is an ERD — the sharpest distractor, since both are produced during database design. The data dictionary documents the meaning and rules of each field, so that a maintainer years later knows what CUST_STAT_3 actually holds.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: The primary advantage of cloud storage over on-premises storage for a growing enterprise is:
options: Guaranteed compliance with the privacy laws of every jurisdiction it operates in
Complete control over the physical hardware and its configuration
Elastic scalability with pay-as-you-go cost and no capital outlay
An assurance that data never leaves the country in which it was collected
questions.explanation: (B) is on-premises' advantage, and (A) and (D) are the opposite of the truth — cloud hosting is what creates the data sovereignty exposure. The counterweights are ongoing subscription cost, dependence on connectivity, vendor lock-in and sovereignty risk.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Data sovereignty means:
options: The enterprise that collected the data owns it outright and may use it freely
Data is subject to the laws of the country in which it is physically stored
Individuals retain the right to control how data about them is used
Governments may compel access to any data held in the cloud
questions.explanation: Australian health data stored on US servers may be reachable under foreign law regardless of Australian contractual promises — which is why many public-sector tenders mandate onshore hosting. (C) is a reasonable-sounding paraphrase of a different idea (data rights).

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an enterprise must:
options: Notify affected individuals and the OAIC of every breach, regardless of likely harm
Notify affected individuals and the OAIC of eligible breaches likely to cause serious harm
Notify the OAIC, which then determines whether individuals should be informed
Publish a public statement describing the breach and the categories of data involved
questions.explanation: The trigger is an eligible data breach likely to result in serious harm — (A) drops that threshold, which is the most commonly chosen wrong answer. Notification must be prompt, and both affected individuals and the OAIC must be told.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: How many Australian Privacy Principles are there under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth)?
options: 7, matching the Privacy by Design principles
10, matching the OECD privacy guidelines
8, matching the ASD Essential Eight
questions.explanation: 13 APPs — , covering open and transparent management, collection, use and disclosure, direct marketing, cross-border disclosure, data quality, security, and access and correction. Each wrong option attaches a real framework to the wrong number.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Since 10 June 2025, Australians have had a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy. Its significance for enterprises is that:
options: It applies only to government agencies and their contracted service providers
Only the OAIC may bring an action, on behalf of the affected individuals
It replaces the Privacy Act as the primary source of privacy obligations
Individuals can sue directly, including entities not otherwise covered by the APPs
questions.explanation: The tort covers intrusion upon seclusion and misuse of information, and reaches parties beyond APP entities — so a small business or an individual can be liable even where the Privacy Act itself would not apply. It sits alongside the Act rather than replacing it.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: From 10 December 2026, Australian privacy policies must disclose:
options: The identity of every third party with whom personal information is shared
The physical location of every server on which personal information is stored
The use of automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals' rights or interests
The retention period applying to each category of personal information collected
questions.explanation: ADM transparency obligations force enterprises to state, in the privacy policy itself, where computers are making consequential decisions about people — directly relevant to credit scoring, recruitment screening and insurance pricing. (A) and (D) are plausible policy contents but are not the new requirement.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: De-identification reduces but does not eliminate privacy risk because:
options: It is reversible by anyone holding the encryption key that was used
The process requires the original identifying data to be retained as a lookup key
De-identified data loses so much detail that it can no longer support useful analysis
Individuals can sometimes be re-identified by linking the dataset with other available data
questions.explanation: Re-identification through linkage attacks is well documented — a few quasi-identifiers (postcode, birth date, sex) are often enough to isolate one person. (A) and (B) describe pseudonymisation, which is a different and weaker technique. Hence suppression of small cells and aggregation before publication.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: The CARE principles for Indigenous data governance stand for:
options: Confidentiality, Availability, Reliability, Efficiency
Consent, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics
Collective benefit, Accessibility, Reusability, Ethics
Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) each substitute one term, and (C) borrows from FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). CARE is people-and-purpose oriented and complements the technically oriented FAIR principles. Related: ICIP — Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Which best describes the 3-2-1 backup rule?
options: Three backups per week, retained for two years, with one full backup monthly
Three copies of the data, on two different media, with one copy encrypted
Three copies of the data, on two different media, with one copy offsite
Three-year retention, followed by two years of archive, then deletion in year one
questions.explanation: (B) changes a single word and is genuinely tempting, but the point of the third element is geographic separation — an encrypted copy in the same building still burns with the building. Modern practice adds an immutable or air-gapped copy to survive ransomware, plus restore testing: an untested backup is not a backup.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: In the CIA triad, integrity means:
options: The origin of the data can be proven and cannot later be denied
Data can be read only by the people authorised to see it
Data is accessible whenever an authorised user needs it
Data is accurate, complete, and has not been improperly altered
questions.explanation: Confidentiality (B) = who can see it; Availability (C) = can you get it when you need it. (A) is non-repudiation, a related property that is not part of the triad. Ransomware attacks availability and integrity simultaneously.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Which is a supervised machine learning task?
options: Predicting whether an email is spam using a labelled training set
Grouping customers into segments with no predefined labels
Reducing a dataset's dimensionality while preserving most of its variance
An agent learning a policy through trial-and-error rewards
questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples in order to predict a known output. (B) and (C) are unsupervised and (D) is reinforcement learning — the presence or absence of labels is the whole test.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: The purpose of holding back a test set is to:
options: Tune the model's hyperparameters before it is finally evaluated
Measure performance on data the model has never seen during training
Increase the volume of data from which the model can learn
Identify and remove outliers before training begins
questions.explanation: (A) is the validation set — a genuinely separate split that catches most people. Evaluating on training data measures memorisation, not generalisation; the validation set tunes hyperparameters, and the test set is touched once, at the very end.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: A model performs excellently on training data and poorly on new data. This is:
options: Underfitting
Overfitting
Data drift
Class imbalance
questions.explanation: Overfitting — the model has learned noise specific to the training set. (C) is the trap when the stem mentions "new data": drift is degradation over time after deployment, whereas overfitting is visible immediately at evaluation. Remedies: more and better data, simpler models, regularisation, cross-validation.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Reinforcement learning is characterised by:
options: A system applying manually coded IF-THEN rules written by domain experts
A model trained on a fully labelled dataset of inputs and their correct outputs
A model grouping unlabelled records into clusters that it discovers for itself
An agent learning a policy through rewards and penalties returned by its environment
questions.explanation: Used in robotics, game playing, dynamic pricing and logistics routing — problems where the right action is revealed only by its consequences over time. (A) is a rule-based expert system: AI, but not machine learning at all.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Over time, a deployed model's accuracy degrades because customer behaviour has changed. This is:
options: Overfitting
Model/data drift
Class imbalance
Underfitting
questions.explanation: Drift — The world moved and the model did not. The tell is over time, after deployment — an overfitted model would have performed poorly on unseen data from day one. Drift is why deployed models need ongoing monitoring and scheduled retraining: an ML system is an operating commitment, not a one-off build.

questions.stem: A logistics enterprise stores GPS telemetry from 800 trucks at one reading per second. Which is the most defensible design decision?
options: Retain readings only for the duration of each trip, then discard them entirely
Stream every reading into the operational database and retain it all indefinitely
Stream every reading into a data lake, relying on governance policy to control later access
Filter and aggregate at the edge, transmit exceptions and hourly summaries, and tier the retention
questions.explanation: It addresses velocity and volume simultaneously, cuts bandwidth and storage cost, and aligns with the obligation to collect and retain only what is necessary. (C) is the sophisticated wrong answer — a lake handles the volume, but keeping every second of driver location indefinitely is exactly the privacy exposure a tiered design avoids. (A) destroys the analytical value the telemetry was collected for.

questions.stem: A hospital's dataset shows a strong correlation between ice-cream sales and drowning incidents. The correct interpretation is:
options: Reverse causation — drowning incidents drive ice-cream sales at the same venues
Ice-cream consumption causes a measurable increase in drowning risk
The correlation is spurious, so the two variables are statistically unrelated
A confounding variable — hot weather — plausibly drives both
questions.explanation: Correlation is not causation. (C) is the trap for anyone who has half-learned the lesson: the correlation is statistically real and reproducible — what is absent is a causal link. (A) names the right category of alternative explanation but the implausible instance of it. Always test for a confounder, mechanistic plausibility, and reverse causation.

questions.stem: An enterprise's marketing and finance teams report different values for "active customers". The most likely root cause is:
options: Inconsistent business definitions applied across separate data sources or marts
One team's extract ran a day earlier than the other's, so the underlying data differs
A referential integrity failure has orphaned some of the customer records
One team applied a filter when building their report that the other did not
questions.explanation: (B) and (D) are genuine operational causes and worth ruling out — but they produce occasional discrepancies, whereas a definitional split produces a persistent one. This is the "one version of the truth" problem. The fix is a governed warehouse with conformed dimensions and a documented, agreed definition of each measure: governance, not technology.

questions.stem: A dataset of 50,000 records has 38% missing values in the "income" field. The most defensible action is:
options: Impute the missing values with the mean of the incomes that were recorded
Drop the field and note the limitation, or impute with a documented method and report the effect
Delete the records with missing income and analyse the remaining 62%
Impute using a model trained on the other fields, then report the results without further comment
questions.explanation: (A) artificially shrinks the variance; (C) is listwise deletion, which is only safe if the missingness is random — and at 38% it almost certainly is not, since high and low earners decline to answer at different rates; (D) uses the best technique but hides it. Whatever you choose, state which and why — undocumented imputation is the real failure.

questions.stem: A supermarket claims its loyalty data proves customers prefer its own brand. The strongest criticism of the sample is:
options: Raw purchase counts do not adjust for the price difference between the brands
Loyalty data is observational, so it cannot establish why customers chose the own brand
The dataset is so large that any difference will register as statistically significant
Loyalty data captures only members' in-store purchases, excluding non-members and competitors' baskets
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (C) are all legitimate criticisms — of the inference, the statistics and the measure respectively — but the question asks about the sample. The sampling frame is the enterprise's own loyal customers, the population most predisposed to agree with the conclusion, so it cannot support a claim about customers generally.

questions.stem: Which statement about metadata retention is correct in a privacy context?
options: Metadata is exempt from the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme
Metadata is not personal information, so it carries no privacy obligations
Metadata such as location, timestamps and contacts can be highly identifying and revealing
Metadata becomes privacy-relevant only once it is linked back to the content it describes
questions.explanation: Who you called, when, from where and how often can reveal more than the call's content ever would — which is exactly why (D) is wrong. Metadata sits squarely within privacy regulation whenever it relates to an identifiable individual.

questions.stem: An enterprise migrating to a data warehouse should perform which check immediately after loading?
options: Compare record counts and control totals between source and target
Rebuild the indexes so that query performance matches the source system
Drop the foreign key constraints so that reporting queries execute faster
Confirm that every field's data type matches its definition in the source system
questions.explanation: (B) and (D) are real post-load activities, but neither would detect the failure that matters most: silent partial loads, where the job reports success having written 80% of the rows. Row counts, checksums and control totals on key measures are the standard reconciliation.

questions.stem: Which is the best justification for using a relational database rather than a spreadsheet for a growing booking system?
options: The database is cheaper to license and to operate at any scale
The database can produce charts and summary reports that a spreadsheet cannot
The database enforces integrity, supports concurrent multi-user access, and scales beyond spreadsheet row limits
The database stores data in compressed form, so it occupies far less disk space
questions.explanation: Concurrency, referential integrity, validation, access control and scale are the structural advantages — and concurrency is usually the decisive one for a booking system, since two people must not book the same slot. Spreadsheets remain excellent for small, single-user, exploratory analysis.

questions.stem: In evaluating a data collection method, which evidence would most strengthen a claim of reliability?
options: Repeating the same instrument on the same population produced consistent results
Subject experts reviewed the instrument and confirmed it measures the intended construct
The sample was drawn randomly and is large enough to represent the population
The results were consistent with the findings of an independent published study
questions.explanation: Reliability = consistency on repetition (test–retest, inter-rater agreement, internal consistency). (B) is evidence of validity and (D) of accuracy — three RAVR criteria, three different kinds of evidence, and the exam rewards knowing which evidence supports which claim.

questions.stem: An enterprise uses AI to screen job applications. Under Australia's Guidance for AI Adoption, the most important governance control is:
options: Removing all demographic fields from the training data before the model is fitted
Human oversight of consequential decisions, plus impact assessment and transparency
Testing the model on a held-out set and publishing the resulting accuracy figure
Encrypting the model file and restricting access to the recruitment team
questions.explanation: (A) is the most tempting and is close to useless: proxy features — suburb, school, career gaps — reconstruct the removed attribute, so fairness must be tested on outcomes, not asserted from an absent input. The six practices are governance and accountability, impact assessment, risk management, transparency, testing and monitoring, and human oversight — with recruitment the paradigm high-impact use case.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest example of secondary use of personal data?
options: Using the delivery address recorded at checkout to deliver the order
Using purchase history collected for order fulfilment to build a health-risk profile sold to a third party
Using purchase history to recommend related products to that same customer
Retaining purchase history for seven years to satisfy tax record-keeping obligations
questions.explanation: (C) is the genuinely borderline case worth understanding: recommending related products is often defensible as a "reasonably expected related purpose" under APP 6, whereas selling an inferred health profile plainly is not. (D) is a use required by other law, not a secondary use.

questions.stem: A data analyst chooses to report the median rather than the mean household income. This is most defensible because:
options: The median can be computed for ordinal data, whereas the mean cannot
The median is less affected by the small number of records with income missing
Income distributions are right-skewed, so the mean is pulled upward by high earners
The mean is not a valid statistic for ratio-level data such as income
questions.explanation: With a skewed distribution the median better represents the typical case. (A) is a true statement about statistics that has no bearing on this question, since income is ratio data — a favourite trap. Reporting both, plus the distribution, is the fullest answer.

questions.stem: An enterprise is deciding between OLTP and OLAP infrastructure for a new executive reporting system. The correct choice and reason is:
options: OLAP, because it stores less data overall and therefore returns results faster
OLTP, because it holds the most current data and is already normalised
OLAP, because it is optimised for complex historical, aggregated queries across dimensions
OLTP, because reporting must not be delayed waiting for the ETL schedule to run
questions.explanation: (D) names a real trade-off — reporting off a warehouse is always slightly stale — but running heavy analytical queries against the operational database degrades the system that is actually running the business. OLTP runs the business (fast small writes, normalised, current); OLAP analyses it (few very large reads, denormalised, historical, multidimensional).

questions.stem: Which action best protects data integrity during collection from a web form?
options: Logging every submission, so incorrect entries can be traced and corrected later
Encrypting the connection, so submitted values cannot be altered in transit
Scheduling a nightly cleaning routine that corrects malformed entries
Applying validation rules — presence, type, range, format, check digit — at the point of entry
questions.explanation: All four are real controls, but they address different problems: (B) protects confidentiality and transmission integrity rather than correctness, and (A) and (C) both accept the bad data first. Preventing bad data at entry is far cheaper than detecting and correcting it afterwards.

questions.stem: A start-up wants to analyse customer sentiment across 200,000 free-text reviews. The most appropriate approach is:
options: Counting keywords, treating any review containing positive words as positive
Natural language processing with sentiment classification, reported directly from the model's output
Manual reading and tallying by a small team of trained coders
Natural language processing with sentiment classification, validated against a human-coded sample
questions.explanation: (B) differs by exactly one clause, and that clause is the whole answer — validating against a human-coded subset is what makes the output defensible rather than merely plausible, and it is where sarcasm, negation and domain slang show up as errors. (C) does not scale to 200,000; (A) is defeated by "not bad" and "hardly great".

questions.stem: An enterprise argues it does not need consent because its data is "publicly available on social media". The strongest counter-argument is:
options: Publicly posted data is unreliable, so consent is needed to verify it with the individual
The platforms' terms of service prohibit third-party collection of user content
Posted content is the platform's copyright, so reusing it requires a licence
Public availability does not remove privacy obligations, and aggregation can create new sensitive inferences
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are real legal arguments, but they are contract and copyright arguments — they would not help the individuals whose privacy is at stake, and they evaporate if the terms change. "It was public" is not a defence for scraping, profiling or re-purposing: scale and aggregation change the nature of the intrusion.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that a data cleaning process was well conducted?
options: Confirmation that the cleaned dataset now contains no missing values, duplicates or impossible values
A summary of how many records were altered and how many removed at each step
A before-and-after comparison of the summary statistics, showing minimal change
A documented, repeatable log of every rule applied, the records affected and the justification, with the raw data preserved unchanged
questions.explanation: (A) is the most attractive wrong answer: it describes a clean outcome, which can equally be produced by deleting everything inconvenient. (C) is confirmation bias dressed as validation — a legitimate clean may well change the statistics. Reproducibility and an untouched raw copy are the hallmarks.

questions.stem: For a small retailer, the strongest argument against adopting a full data warehouse is:
options: A warehouse cannot integrate data from more than one source system
Build cost, ETL complexity and maintenance overhead exceed the analytical benefit at that data volume
A warehouse holds historical data, so it cannot support day-to-day operational decisions
A warehouse requires data to be moved offshore, creating data sovereignty exposure
questions.explanation: (C) is a half-truth worth untangling: a warehouse is the wrong tool for operational transactions, but that is a reason to keep the OLTP system, not an argument against having a warehouse as well. Right-sizing the solution is a genuine EC-12-08 judgement — a well-structured relational database plus a BI tool may deliver 90% of the value at 10% of the cost.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the analytics pipeline?
options: Collect → clean/transform → store → analyse → visualise → decide
Collect → analyse → clean/transform → store → visualise → decide
Collect → store → visualise → clean/transform → analyse → decide
Collect → clean/transform → store → visualise → analyse → decide
questions.explanation: (D) is the fine distinction — visualisation communicates the result of analysis, so reversing them means presenting a picture before you know what it shows. Note the pipeline is iterative: discovering a quality problem at the analysis stage sends you back to collection, not forward to visualisation.

questions.stem: An enterprise claims its ML model is "objective because it removes human judgement". The best critique is:
options: Human judgement is embedded in the choice of training data, features, labels and success metric — the model automates those judgements rather than removing them
Models are less accurate than experienced human assessors performing the same task
Objectivity requires the model's source code to be published for independent review
The model's outputs vary between runs, so its decisions are not reproducible
questions.explanation: Every model encodes a chain of human decisions — most consequentially the choice of what counts as success. The danger is that automation launders those judgements into apparent neutrality and then applies them at scale, which is precisely what makes algorithmic bias so hard to challenge.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: A spreadsheet cell contains 2170. Which additional fact would be sufficient to classify it as ratio data?
options: It is the number of litres of fuel purchased in a transaction
It is the postcode of the customer's billing address
It is stored as a number rather than as text
It is the year in which the account was opened
questions.explanation: Ratio requires a true zero, so arithmetic including ratios is meaningful — zero litres means none. A postcode is nominal, a calendar year is interval (year 0 is arbitrary), and the storage type is irrelevant to the level of measurement.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: Which pair of values could not validly be averaged?
options: Response times in seconds for 40 support tickets
Daily maximum temperatures in degrees Celsius across a month
Annual revenue figures for six branches
Customer satisfaction recorded as Poor / Fair / Good / Excellent
questions.explanation: Ordinal categories have order but unequal intervals, so the mean assumes a precision the data does not carry. Celsius is interval — the mean is valid even though ratios are not, which is the distinction most often confused here.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: An enterprise argues that because star ratings are stored as integers 1–5, the mean rating is a valid KPI. The strongest counter is:
options: The intervals between adjacent ratings are not demonstrably equal, so the mean implies a precision the scale lacks
Ratings must be converted to percentages before any statistic is calculated
Star ratings are nominal, so only the mode may be reported
The mean is only valid for continuous data, and integers are discrete
questions.explanation: Star ratings are ordinal. They are not nominal — the order is real — which is why (C) overstates the objection, and the discrete/continuous distinction in (D) is a separate issue that does not by itself invalidate a mean.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: Which is the clearest example of information rather than data?
options: A log file containing 40,000 timestamped page requests
The value 00:04:12 recorded against session 88214
"Average session duration fell 18% after the checkout redesign"
A database table of every completed transaction this quarter
questions.explanation: Information is data processed, organised and given context so it carries meaning. The others are raw facts — large volume does not make data into information, which is the trap in (A) and (D).

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: In the DIKW model, the step from knowledge to wisdom is best characterised as:
options: Applying judgement about what should be done, including when not to act
Aggregating individual records into summary statistics
Adding context so the data becomes meaningful
Storing the processed output in a data warehouse for reuse
questions.explanation: Data → information adds context, information → knowledge adds understanding of patterns and causes, knowledge → wisdom adds judgement and values. (C) describes the first step, not the last.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: Which dataset is semi-structured?
options: An XML feed where optional elements appear only in some records
A normalised relational table with enforced data types
A folder of scanned invoices stored as JPEG images
A CSV export with a fixed header row and consistent columns
questions.explanation: Semi-structured data carries tags or markers but no rigid schema. A CSV is structured despite being a flat file — the trap is assuming "not a database" means "not structured".

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: An enterprise says 85% of its data is unstructured. The most significant analytical consequence is:
options: The data cannot be stored economically
The data has no metadata and therefore cannot be catalogued
SQL alone cannot interrogate it, so NLP, computer vision or ML techniques are required
The data must be discarded after its retention period expires
questions.explanation: Unstructured data usually has rich metadata, so (B) is false. Storage is cheap; the barrier is that the query tools most enterprises own cannot read it.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: Which variable is interval rather than ratio?
options: Time taken to complete a task, in minutes
Weight of a parcel in kilograms
Number of items in a shopping basket
IQ score
questions.explanation: IQ — The scale has order and (by construction) equal intervals, but its zero is arbitrary — an IQ of 140 is not "twice as intelligent" as 70. The others all have a genuine zero.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: A researcher codes free-text complaints into themes and counts how often each theme appears. The resulting counts are:
options: Qualitative data, because the source material was qualitative
Quantitative data at the nominal level, since the themes are unordered labels being counted
Ordinal data, because some themes are more serious than others
Invalid, because qualitative data cannot be counted
questions.explanation: Thematic coding produces nominal categories, and frequency counts of those categories are legitimate quantitative analysis. (A) is the common error — the analysis, not the source, determines the type.

questions.topic: Data, information and levels of measurement
questions.stem: The strongest justification for a mixed-methods approach is that:
options: Quantitative data establishes what is happening while qualitative data explains why
It doubles the sample size and therefore halves the margin of error
Qualitative data is more reliable than quantitative data
It satisfies the requirement to collect both active and passive data
questions.explanation: (B) confuses two separate datasets with one larger sample, and (D) invents a requirement — active/passive is a collection taxonomy, not a methodological obligation.

questions.stem: A hotel places a tablet at reception inviting departing guests to rate their stay. This is:
options: Computerised and passive, because a device records the response
Manual and passive, because no interviewer is present
Manual and active, because a staff member prompts the guest
Computerised and active, because the guest knowingly participates
questions.explanation: The axis is knowing participation, not whether a human is present. The device makes it computerised; the guest's deliberate response makes it active.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant limitation of passive collection for an enterprise investigating why customers churn?
options: The data volume is too small to support statistical analysis
It requires explicit consent from every customer before collection
It cannot be timestamped, so trends cannot be established
It records behaviour but cannot capture motivation or reasoning
questions.explanation: Passive collection typically produces more data, not less, and it is routinely timestamped. Its structural gap is the missing why — which is exactly what a churn investigation needs.

questions.stem: An enterprise samples every 20th customer from a list sorted by signup date. The specific risk is:
options: Periodic bias, if a cycle in the list coincides with the sampling interval
Volunteer bias, since customers self-select into the sample
Coverage bias, since the sampling frame excludes non-customers
Response bias, since customers may answer to please the interviewer
questions.explanation: This is systematic sampling. (C) is true of any customer list but is not caused by the method; the method-specific hazard is a periodic pattern aligning with the interval.

questions.stem: A researcher needs to guarantee that a 4% minority group is represented proportionally. The correct method is:
options: Stratified sampling with the group as its own stratum
Simple random sampling with a large enough sample
Cluster sampling by geographic region
Systematic sampling with a small interval
questions.explanation: Random sampling makes proportional representation likely but does not guarantee it — that word is what rules out (B). Stratification enforces it by construction.

questions.stem: Cluster sampling is chosen primarily because it:
options: Reduces cost and logistical difficulty when the population is geographically dispersed
Produces a smaller margin of error than simple random sampling
Removes the need for a sampling frame entirely
Guarantees each subgroup is represented in proportion to its size
questions.explanation: It trades precision for practicality — members within a cluster tend to be similar, so sampling error is higher for the same sample size, which is the opposite of (B).

questions.stem: Which finding would most strongly indicate a problem with validity rather than reliability?
options: Two researchers using the same instrument produce different results
The survey measures brand awareness but is being used to conclude purchase intent
The instrument produces the same wrong reading every time
Repeating the survey next month produces very different answers
questions.explanation: Validity is about measuring the right construct. (A) and (D) are reliability failures, and (C) is the classic reliable-but-inaccurate case.

questions.stem: A dataset is highly accurate and highly reliable but was collected in 2015 for a question about current behaviour. The failing criterion is:
options: Reliability
Accuracy
Relevance
Validity
questions.explanation: Relevance — whether the data actually relates to the question being asked. Age is a relevance problem here rather than an accuracy one; the 2015 figures may be perfectly correct for 2015.

questions.stem: Which is a transposition error rather than a transcription error?
options: Entering Smith as Smyth
Entering $1,450 as $14,50
Leaving a required field blank
Entering 4821 as 4281
questions.explanation: Transposition = characters swapped. (B) is a misplaced separator and (A) a mistyping — both transcription errors. Check digits are designed specifically to catch (D).

questions.stem: A "presence check" would catch which of the following?
options: A price entered as twelve dollars
An email address entered without an @
A date of birth of 2099-01-01
A required phone number field left empty
questions.explanation: Presence = is there anything here. (C) needs a range check, (B) a format check and (A) a type check — all four are validation, which is why the distractors are close.

questions.stem: Validation confirms an entered customer address is correctly formatted and plausible. It cannot confirm that:
options: The postcode field contains four digits
The address is the one where the customer actually lives
The state field contains a recognised abbreviation
The field is not empty
questions.explanation: Validation tests form and reasonableness, not truth. Confirming the value matches the source is verification, and confirming it matches reality needs an external check.

questions.stem: A sensor drifts out of calibration and records every reading 4% high. This is best described as:
options: An outlier problem requiring winsorisation
Random error, which cancels out across a large sample
Systematic measurement bias, which does not cancel out
A transcription error introduced at the data entry stage
questions.explanation: The critical property is that a systematic offset persists no matter how large the sample grows — which is precisely why (B) is wrong and why more data does not fix bias.

questions.stem: An analyst removes all values more than three standard deviations from the mean before reporting. The strongest objection is:
options: Standard deviation cannot be calculated on ratio data
The rule may delete genuine extremes that carry the most important signal, and the deletion is undocumented
Outliers should always be replaced with the median instead
Three standard deviations is too wide a threshold to remove anything
questions.explanation: Fraud, equipment failure and the best customer all look like outliers. The defensible practice is investigate, decide, and document — not apply a rule silently.

questions.stem: Which is confirmation bias rather than selection bias?
options: Excluding records with missing values without checking why they are missing
Surveying only customers who opened the marketing email
Recruiting participants at a shopping centre on a weekday morning
Stopping data collection once the results support the expected conclusion
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias operates on the analyst's decisions about evidence. (B) and (C) shape the sample; (A) is a cleaning decision that can create bias but is not confirmation bias.

questions.stem: Records with missing income values turn out to be concentrated among low-income respondents. Deleting those rows would:
options: Have no effect, since the remaining data is complete
Reduce reliability but not introduce bias
Introduce bias, because the missingness is related to the value itself
Be acceptable provided the deletion is documented
questions.explanation: Missingness that correlates with the underlying value is not random, so deleting shifts the distribution. Documentation (D) is necessary but does not repair the distortion.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of metadata creating a privacy risk without any content being exposed?
options: A leaked spreadsheet of customer email addresses
A published dashboard of aggregate regional sales
Call records showing who contacted a crisis helpline, when, and from where
A backup file encrypted with an outdated algorithm
questions.explanation: No conversation content is revealed, yet the pattern is highly sensitive and identifying. (A) is content, not metadata — the distinction the question tests.

questions.stem: A dataset described as "primary" for one enterprise becomes "secondary" when:
options: It is more than 12 months old
It is reused by a different party for a different purpose
It is aggregated to protect privacy
It is transferred into a data warehouse
questions.explanation: Primary/secondary describes the relationship between the collector and the user, not the age, location or state of processing of the data.

questions.stem: A convenience sample of 12,000 responses and a random sample of 800 both address the same question. The random sample is preferable because:
options: Smaller samples are less prone to data entry error
Sample size cannot compensate for a sample that is systematically unrepresentative
Random sampling removes response bias as well as selection bias
Convenience samples cannot be analysed statistically
questions.explanation: This is the central lesson of sampling: bias does not shrink with n. (C) overclaims — random selection addresses who is chosen, not how honestly they answer.

questions.stem: Which action would most improve the reliability of a data collection instrument?
options: Increasing the sample size
Adding an open-ended comment field
Cross-checking a subset of records against an authoritative source
Standardising the wording, order and administration of every question
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency on repetition, so it is improved by controlling the procedure. (C) improves accuracy, and (A) affects precision of estimates rather than instrument consistency.

questions.stem: An enterprise cleans a dataset by standardising "NSW", "N.S.W." and "New South Wales" to a single value. This is:
options: Data cleaning through standardisation of formats
Verification, since values are checked against the source
Validation, since inconsistent values are rejected
De-identification, since the specific value is generalised
questions.explanation: Nothing is rejected and nothing is checked against a source, which rules out the first two; and generalising a state does not de-identify anyone.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest indicator that a survey suffers from response bias?
options: The response rate was 8%
Self-reported exercise minutes far exceed measured activity for the same respondents
Responses were collected only through the mobile app
Some respondents skipped the income question
